L-abstract-algebra.statement: Luthier has to do with abstract algebra.

L-abstraction-mechanism.statement: Luthier is an abstraction mechanism, a relator, for expressing ideas clearly (probability, sample, matrix, units, experiment).

L-accumulates-without-advancing.statement: Luthier keeps accumulating ideas without starting to advance, tending to grow to encompass the universe, attractive but like a bag of gas.

L-adjoint-forward-diagnostic.statement: Each forward operation (simulate, infer) is paired by adjunction with a diagnostic approximation (recover, summarize).

L-algebraic-and-semantic.statement: Luthier should have a very algebraic way of writing itself that can express almost anything like a universal Turing machine, yet where each element is semantically defined and understandable by humans.

L-almacen-is-constructor-function.statement: A structure like Almacen is a function that takes the raw operations and returns the verified versions, so the only way to obtain one is to pass the check.

L-apply-luthier-to-databaum.statement: Luthier's concepts (function plus version, a table of functions) are carried into the design of the analysis/derivation store.

L-arena-or-lambda-calculus.statement: Luthier can grow as a universal arena or, more simply, as a down-to-earth lambda calculus.

L-ascii-canonical.statement: The canonical form of the language is ASCII; an editor may display -> as an arrow or * as a cross, but what is run by hand and grepped is the ASCII.

L-based-on-hott.statement: Build Luthier to map strictly onto homotopy type theory, with very few types following its small set of well-defined rules.

L-bayesian-complexity-estimate.statement: The a priori complexity of implementations is estimated by a Bayesian strategy: give chances to different algorithms, measure their actual times, and estimate from accumulated experience.

L-bayesian-mapping.statement: Scientific knowledge production is mapped into explicit Bayesian structures (introduction to prior, methods to likelihood, results to observations, discussion to posterior) to make reasoning auditable and probabilistic.

L-block-is-program.statement: Braces delimit a block that can hold local definitions; a block is a Program with one definition marked as output, giving local definitions without new primitives.

L-bootstrap-pact.statement: The only thing outside Luthier is a bootstrap that accepts a Program value, parses it and runs eval; once eval written in Luthier runs on itself the bootstrapper can be discarded, which is the concrete self-extensibility.

L-bridge-language.statement: Luthier should be minimal, essentially a bridge language connecting other languages.

L-build-before-it-falls.statement: Luthier must be built now, before access to highly qualified AI guidance becomes restricted.

L-butler-orchestrator.statement: Luthier is a higher-order language, a butler that orchestrates other languages, runs programs, compares their outputs, and chooses where to run each computation.

L-candidate-named-not-forall.statement: The candidate value is named and the laws applied to it explicitly, but it has the material's type (naming it by the subtype is circular) and needs no forall; the sample size is certificate data, not part of the type.

L-category-style-basics.statement: The basic elements are defined in category-theory style, functors from arrows, out of a few basal elements.

L-certificate-clause-with-hypotheses.statement: A certificate is a clause with hypotheses (H1 and ... and Hn imply L), and a program's certificate is the closure of those clauses, which gives composition its exact meaning.

L-certificate-first-class.statement: The certificate is a first-class value carrying its level of guarantee, composable and forgettable, accumulating by composition across values, functions and programs, with runs persisted as data.

L-check-infer-bidirectional.statement: check traverses the definitions verifying each type is a type and each body has its declared type, infer computes the type by recursion over Term, and real verifiers are bidirectional, which is where refl types or not.

L-check-value-vs-function.statement: Checking a value is an exact computation and checking a function is sampling, but both are the same construct operation differing only in whether the check is exact or statistical.

L-class-carries-structure.statement: A class should generate and carry its structure and give access to its records, rather than being a bare simple structure.

L-closed-observer.statement: Luthier is a closed, internally complete universe that observes the outside through a read/write boundary which is also a compilation.

L-code-enables-autodiff.statement: Code that represents the calculations can be autodifferentiated and yield a step-by-step written result.

L-code-is-data.statement: Code is data, erasing the distinction between code and data, following the Lisp model.

L-code-many-operations.statement: Luthier code is not merely compiled and run; many operations apply to it (verify, compile, run), giving more complexity but more expressivity.

L-code-obeys-laws-not-floats.statement: Floating-point numbers do not obey the algebraic laws of numbers, but the code is assumed to, so it can be reorganized for efficiency.

L-code-operations.statement: The language builds in functions that operate on code: tests, errors, derivatives, finding equivalents, and timing.

L-code-to-understand.statement: He codes to understand, which means being able to manipulate the code and see how changes affect its observables.

L-collaborative-filtering.statement: Use matrix factorization / collaborative filtering to predict an algorithm's runtime on an input.

L-coloneq-act-vs-equiv.statement: := is the act of giving a name a body, while ≡ is the larger relation that follows from all the := plus the computation rules (lambda substitution, recursor rules); "true by definition" broadly means true by unfolding and computing.

L-commutative-program.statement: An open question is whether a Luthier program is commutative in the order of its statements, and how to model time/order; declarations can be near-commutative.

L-commuting-squares.statement: Coherence of forgetting and applying functions is analyzed with commuting squares: the two paths are compared for equivalence.

L-compare-equivalent-paths.statement: Luthier compares two paths that do the same thing and determines they are equivalent, possibly with format-conversion stages at the start and end.

L-compile-time-prevents-invalid.statement: The type system prevents invalid models from being constructed, eliminating consistency violations at compile time before execution or inference.

L-compiler-is-prover.statement: Letting functions return types makes the Luthier compiler a mathematical prover, so code and its proof become the same thing.

L-compiling-detects-errors.statement: Compiling is checking whether the code holds incompatible things; unlike algebraic calculation, many programs should not compile, because that is how errors are caught.

L-compose-programs.statement: Luthier composes the input and output of one program with another, chaining external programs.

L-compose-programs-harmonically.statement: The fundamental problem is how Luthier programs connect and expand one another so they grow harmonically, with incompatibilities possible.

L-composition-dot.statement: Composition is written with a dot, which explains class methods.

L-compositional-kinetic.statement: Kinetic models are built compositionally from conformational state components as an external product of degrees of freedom with energetic coupling rules and state aggregation.

L-computation-categories.statement: There are categories of computations that take the same time for different inputs, and these classes must be found so not every computation need be measured.

L-concept-first.statement: The first step is expressing concepts in Luthier with conceptual depth; the translation/implementation comes after.

L-concept-is-a-function.statement: A concept needs no new type: it is an ordinary function returning a type (with proofs) or a list of laws (with tests).

L-concept-is-predicate-over-functions.statement: A concept is a predicate over functions, a list of requirements, so two implementations satisfying it are interchangeable.

L-concepts-independent-or-tied.statement: Some concepts can live independently of their container (like a mean) while others are intrinsically tied to one (like an iteration to its algorithm).

L-concrete-to-luthier-problem.statement: A concrete implementation need is used to surface the underlying Luthier design problem.

L-construction-pattern-is-core.statement: The core of Luthier is one construction pattern: from a material type and a predicate over it derive a certified type, a validating constructor and the forgetful projection to the material, the same for values, functions and whole programs.

L-constructor-vs-function.statement: A constructor differs from a function in that a constructor plus its parameters is the element, making elements transparent, while a function involves a computation.

L-constructors-in-type-space.statement: Constructors should live in each type's space rather than in the global space.

L-contagiously-safe-dsl.statement: A compile-time safe model DSL whose safety is contagious, propagating through the system via the compiler, with backend codegen, as the endgame of HoTTification.

L-context-as-dag.statement: The program/context is modeled as a Directed Acyclic Graph of definitions where types depend on others, and operating on Luthier is combining DAGs via substitution.

L-core-five-pieces.statement: The core is five pieces (the definition with the hole, lambda calculus with reduction, U, Π, data); from data come Σ, =, ⊥, ⊤, N, Program, while Bayes, the run database and numbers-with-error stay outside as libraries.

L-core-library-sugar-layers.statement: The language is three layers: a small core (a handful of term forms plus data, definition and reduction, a ten-line EBNF with reserved words data, match, extern), a base library written in Luthier, and sugar whose translation is mechanical; no Bool, numbers, =, Sigma or Subtype in the core.

L-core-plus-libraries.statement: Luthier is a closed core plus libraries, the libraries being Luthier functions that connect it to external programs.

L-correlated-data-worth-more.statement: Correlated data are worth more than isolated data, and larger patterns need ever more data.

L-couple-to-sonolocalizacion.statement: Luthier is a meta-project whose next development couples to sonolocalización at the library (and MacroIR) stage, and how to relate the two remains to be worked out.

L-coupled-functions-product.statement: When a law couples several functions, the material is their product and the pattern unpacks it to name each component, so the laws are written over named components.

L-couplings-as-types.statement: Energetic couplings, binding schemes and conformational spaces are represented and certified as types.

L-create-objects-uniformly.statement: The language expresses and creates values, variables, types and functions uniformly, with their semantics.

L-cross-language.statement: Luthier is not tied to one language but a pseudo-language implementable across languages (cross-language, not cross-compiler), with its engine in one and PyLuthier/RLuthier/CLuthier transformable into one another.

L-data-gives-recursor.statement: A data declaration gives three things: the type, the constructors (ordinary bodyless functions in normal form), and the recursor (one case per constructor with a reduction rule each); every function over the type is an instance of this recursor.

L-data-sum-of-products.statement: A data is a sum of products plus recursion (sum between constructors, product inside each, recursion as least fixpoint), so data is primitive and + and × are its degenerate cases.

L-date-both-consolidations.statement: The May consolidation is kept by renaming and dating both versions so the ecosystem's evolution can be compared.

L-declarative-and-optimizer.statement: Luthier is at once a declarative language and an optimization tool: you declare what you want and it openly shuffles implementations, a map between a declarative language and an executive one.

L-decompose-components.statement: A first task is to understand all the things Luthier currently groups together, to see which are functionally separable and which depend on which.

L-decorator-algebra.statement: Decorators should be easy to express, and one asks whether composing them is associative or commutative, representing the simplest form when it is.

L-decorators-error.statement: Decorators express the error of a number and its propagation (derivatives), as he did in C++ with templates.

L-define-invariants.statement: Defining an invariant f : A -> B with for-all x : A, g x (f x) where g : A -> B -> Bool: the for-all is the Π, g's Bool is lifted to a proposition via a data Cierto : Bool -> U, and the invariant ties to f either as a separate hole-definition (the declaration is the test) or as a package where the guarantee travels with the function.

L-definition-form-depends-on-type.statement: The form of a definition, how its clauses are written, may depend on reducing its type, the same definitional equality at work.

L-definition-fundamental.statement: The most fundamental element of a program is not the type or the function but the definition, name : Type := term; a program is a finite unordered set of definitions and the DAG comes from which names each uses.

L-definition-is-its-test.statement: Defining a function defines its test (its inverse, its simulation), so running the code runs the test.

L-definitional-equality.statement: "True by definition" is definitional equality ≡ (two terms reducing to the same normal form), a judgment the reducer decides, distinct from =, the identity type whose terms are paths, making "the test is the code" literal.

L-delegate-execution.statement: Luthier might delegate execution entirely and do only verification, as extreme minimalism.

L-dep-types-composition.statement: Hierarchical, algebraic model composition across subunits, pathways and scales is enforced by dependent types.

L-dep-types-semantic-safety.statement: Dependent typing enforces semantic safety, guaranteeing the internal consistency of model compositions.

L-dependent-types-as-type-returning.statement: A dependent type is a function that returns a type instead of a value, raising the level of abstraction.

L-dependent-types-basic.statement: Dependent types are probably one of the language's basic initial concepts.

L-dependent-types-def.statement: Dependent types are types that depend on a value, taking the cardinality of that value's type.

L-derived-is-proof-term.statement: A derived object, the tuple of inputs, function, parameters and result, is a proof term whose type is the proposition that the result was obtained that way, making the base a store of proofs.

L-derived-never-edited.statement: A derived object is never edited; corrections are human assertions that are themselves originals, putting labels, quality control and corrections in the same place.

L-description-language.statement: Luthier's first stage is a language for describing the problem, the functions and the conditions under which they work, not for execution.

L-dot-separator.statement: The dot in Σ (x : X). A x is a notational separator marking where the bound variable ends and the body begins, the same dot as in λ and Π, like the brace in f(x) { ... }, and one convention should serve all three binders.

L-double-definition.statement: A type defined twice could be flagged as error or read as a cartesian product that runs two ways.

L-dsl-as-model-compiler.statement: The DSLs are model compilers that translate high-level mechanistic specifications into executable, inferable structures.

L-dsl-kernel-yaml.statement: A DSL kernel gives a declarative model interface in YAML, isolating the model interface from the C++ internals.

L-dsl-unifies-domains.statement: One DSL framework unifies models across channels, enzymes, networks, signaling and regulation.

L-dynamic-naming.statement: For dynamically created types or functions, a name is really an address, so a generated numeric identifier suffices.

L-easy-delegation.statement: Delegation should be easy in Luthier, an idea he traces to Modelica.

L-element-belongs-one-type.statement: Each element belongs to exactly one type but can serve to build many types.

L-embedded-semantic-structure.statement: Biological models carry embedded semantic structure such as symmetry groups, compositional operators and equivalence classes.

L-encode-as-types.statement: Model components, entities and deterministic structure are encoded as types.

L-encode-epistemic-structure.statement: Scientific code should encode its epistemic structure as executable epistemology, with verification semantic rather than syntactic and type safety arising from epistemic clarity.

L-environment-first-object.statement: The environment is the first object the language must define, since data is loaded into it.

L-environment-kinds.statement: There are simple environments (one value type, one identifier) and compound ones that admit multiple.

L-environment-resources.statement: The environment needs and manages resources (memory and compute) and function execution, a problem that ties to it but exceeds it (OS, compiler).

L-environment-stores-retrieves.statement: The environment is a map of definitions whose two mechanisms are storing and retrieving variables by name.

L-epistemic-compression.statement: A few adjunction-derived tests cover most of the risk; verification is compressed into a minimal, epistemically meaningful suite.

L-epistemic-firewall.statement: The SAV verification layer acts as an epistemic firewall defending the system against silent semantic drift during refactoring.

L-equality-symbols.statement: Equality gets distinct symbols: := defines (an asymmetric act), = is the identity type (the proposition), == is library decidable equality, and ≡, the definitional one, is not written in programs.

L-equals-assertion.statement: The equals sign is an assertion that both sides are equal, also used for pattern matching when a symbol is unknown.

L-essential-vs-decoration.statement: Function equivalences separate what is essential (the equivalent) from what is decoration (efficiency, cost), the non-equivalent.

L-ev-sugar-syntax.statement: The sugar that stores an evaluation needs delimiters and always stores, since the context cannot decide its type and keeping only failures is the test's filter, not a property of the evaluation.

L-eval-fuel.statement: eval repeating a step is not structural recursion and need not terminate, so it is given fuel, eval : N -> Program -> Term -> Maybe Term, making it total, and how much fuel was needed is the first cost measure for free.

L-evaluation-storage-object.statement: The object storing a function, its argument and its result is the graph of evaluation (Ev f), with a sugar that evaluates and stores it; evalstore is just that pair, not a third operation, and the run base is a list of them.

L-evidence-in-sigma.statement: Being more specific with types means types are data and knowledge about a value is carried as an evidence component in a Σ, marked erasable, but with the evidence sometimes written and kept and the erasable mark set by whoever defines.

L-executable-by-hand.statement: If well written, Luthier should be executable by hand with pencil and paper, like Lisp.

L-execute-when-defined.statement: Code is not executed until it is fully defined, so undefined dead code can sit there without bothering anyone.

L-execution-as-forgetting.statement: Execution is a forgetful function: code generates code, with one level that keeps the generated code and one that forgets it.

L-execution-is-verification.statement: Execution in Luthier is the verification of equivalences, as mathematics does not execute but only verifies equivalences.

L-express-alternatives.statement: The point is not to do everything but to have the tools to express different alternatives; no option is best or worst, and even expressing something to discard it has value.

L-express-extracomputational.statement: The language expresses extra-computational concepts like probability by abstracting their properties and verifying compliance (e.g. a probability lies in [0,1]).

L-express-invariances.statement: Luthier's aim is to express the invariances of the disciplines (a species mates within itself; electrons are fermions, photons bosons).

L-express-math-structures.statement: The language must express mathematical structures (category, functor, group) with their laws, possibly in several declaration styles.

L-express-then-execute.statement: You first express the ideas with pencil and paper and then go to execution or the empirical database; these are two layers, not opposed philosophies.

L-expressiveness.statement: Code must express its intention to both the human reader and the compiler, referring truthfully to known structures.

L-expressivity-vs-redundancy.statement: A choice between redundancy (robustness) and expressivity; he prefers expressivity with good compiler messages, since redundancy can needlessly limit.

L-external-element.statement: Everything that is not Luthier (C++, Python, the machine, any resource) is modeled as its own kind of external element.

L-first-class-contexts.statement: The context could be treated as a type in itself, what theory calls first-class contexts.

L-fisher-validation.statement: A likelihood implementation is validated by agreement between the Fisher Information Matrix from score covariance and the one from the Hessian, without full inference.

L-forgetful-functors.statement: Which forgetting function you apply to the types defines the language you speak; forgetful functors are among Luthier's most important components, and different ones optimize different things.

L-forgetting-affects-precision.statement: How much of the operational history is kept determines the recoverable numerical precision, tying the forget functor to precision.

L-forgetting-in-hott.statement: The concept of forgetting (a type forgetting parts of the type) is already present in HoTT.

L-forgetting-is-fst.statement: Forgetting is fst of a Σ, and what to forget is library policy.

L-forgetting-problem.statement: The forgetting problem, controlling the typing information that grows as types compose, is one of Luthier's fundamental problems to solve.

L-formalize-state-energy-algebra.statement: Planned work to formalize a type system for state and energy algebra and HoTT-based state composition primitives.

L-formers-are-primitive.statement: Elementary types and functions are not primitive; the primitives are the formers (U, Π, data), with N defined by data, R a structure with axioms and seno a hole.

L-forms-of-definition.statement: The language distinguishes declaration from definition and lets one define functions or variables by their type without giving the implementation or value (parameters).

L-forward-and-undefined-types.statement: A type may be referenced before it is defined and defined later, or left undefined, in which case it is a program input.

L-foundation-choice.statement: Open question of which foundation to build on (type theory vs category theory, HoTT vs ZMT).

L-function-by-properties.statement: A function can be defined by its properties, the propositions its inputs and outputs satisfy, not only operationally, keeping both.

L-function-deterministic.statement: If the identity of a derived object is its inputs, function, version and parameters, the function must be deterministic: seed and environment enter as explicit arguments, or the certificate lies.

L-function-holds-code.statement: A function holds its code written in the language plus a compiled simplified form.

L-function-kinds.statement: Functions are of two kinds: predefined and user defined.

L-function-type-expression.statement: Open question of how to express the type of a function such as write : a -> string.

L-functor-as-implementation.statement: A functor is read as an implementation and a natural transformation as translating one implementation into another.

L-fundamental-elements-question.statement: What are the most fundamental elements of a program? Candidates: elementary types, elementary functions, code versus data, true/false, true-by-definition, address/data.

L-gap-of-usefulness.statement: The method is to find the gap of usefulness, a concrete place from which Luthier can begin to develop while being useful.

L-generalize-database.statement: The performance database must be generalizable from point measurements to trends, e.g. estimating an empty cell from its row and column averages or something more sophisticated.

L-generic-concept-contextualized.statement: A concept like status or iteration can be a generic class, with the particular algorithm it belongs to known from its containing context and carried as an identifier.

L-grammar-parallel.statement: Natural-language grammatical categories parallel programming constructs, a frame for choosing Luthier's primitives.

L-groupoid-structure.statement: Inference operations and their diagnostics form equivalence classes, a pre-formal groupoid structure.

L-higher-paths-symmetries.statement: Higher-order symmetries and transformations between equivalences are captured as higher paths.

L-hijack-code.statement: Luthier must be able to hijack code from any other language.

L-hole-five-roles.statement: The hole, a definition with a type and no body, plays five roles at once (axiom, program input, external function, pending definition, dead code), and "you don't execute until it's defined" is its exact semantics, removing the need for an External type.

L-hole-goal-messages.statement: A hole inside a term lets the verifier accept what is written and state the exact type of what is missing (Agda's goal), which is the compiler with good messages about what is happening.

L-hole-needs-no-symbol.statement: The hole needs no symbol in the core: a bodyless declaration f : A → B is already a hole, an opaque name that doesn't reduce, and ? is derivable surface sugar.

L-hole-no-intention.statement: The core does not distinguish why a hole has no body (to be filled externally or just unwritten); huecos : Program → List Name lists them all and intention goes in the definition's text field.

L-hot-values-paths.statement: Hot values open a larger universe of possible paths than ordinary values.

L-hott-dsl-for-biology.statement: Build a domain-specific modeling language on Homotopy Type Theory for expressing, composing and transforming biological models with access to type-level structure.

L-hott-ingredients-sufficient.statement: Sigma-types, Pi-types, identity types and HITs suffice to encode conformational models, energetic couplings and symmetry structures.

L-hott-not-probabilistic.statement: HoTT does not work on probabilities, though probabilities could be built within it; the defect is that it is not native.

L-hott-prob-tension.statement: There is a tension between HoTT's invertible identities and univalence and probability's non-invertible uncertainty, with no fully unified model yet.

L-hottification-definition.statement: HoTTification is transforming a scientific model, algorithm or modeling language into a formal structure governed by HoTT, analogous to categorification or quantization.

L-hottification-models-typed-objects.statement: Under HoTTification models themselves become typed mathematical objects whose equivalences, symmetries and compositions are validated by the type system.

L-hottification-roadmap.statement: HoTTification is a staged program, a semantic elevation not a rewrite, running from SAV diagnostics through DSL/CLI modularization and wrappers to a full homotopical, type-theoretic kernel.

L-identifier-type-independent.statement: The identifier and the type are completely independent; the identifier is a fantasy name unknown until resolved.

L-identifiers-central.statement: Identifiers are central: a simple label recovers a complex object, the dictionary joining human and machine.

L-identity-paths-equivalences.statement: Identity paths represent structural equivalences between model entities.

L-implementation-of-concept.statement: A Luthier definition should determine uniquely that a concrete computation is an implementation of a concept (e.g. of matrices).

L-implicit-types.statement: Types can be defined implicitly, as the solution to a problem or the optimum of a function, rather than declared directly.

L-indexed-data-families.statement: Indexed constructors whose return type carries an index (Vec : N -> U) are a further layer of data, letting a type like Traza t u have constructors only for pairs that really reduce to one another.

L-infectability-lens.statement: Consolidation uses infectability as its lens: the ideas that most change how you program are the ones that most structure the language; it is a project-specific choice.

L-inject-multiple-identifiers.statement: A type or function can inject more than one identifier into the environment.

L-invariant-is-bool-function-field.statement: In version 0 an invariant is a function returning Bool, stored as a field of the definition beside the body, with a generator hole filled by type and the run kept as data.

L-inventory-cpp-constructs.statement: An inventory of C++ constructs (classes, functions, enums, structs, templates, pointers, references, derived classes, polymorphism) as what exists and must be selected from.

L-judgment-depends-on-type.statement: a : A is a judgment, not a proposition, and what it means depends on the kind of type A is (a mere proposition: A holds and a is how I know; a set: a is one of A's elements).

L-juxtaposition-application.statement: Application is written by juxtaposition f a and binds tighter than any operator, so f(a) is the same, f a b is curried and f (a, b) applies to a pair, the two coexisting as distinct types, with multiplication explicit.

L-know-that-vs-which.statement: The distinction to keep is knowing that (a mere proposition's proof) versus knowing which (a set's value); the passage from the second to the first is truncation, the most basic forgetting, where the forget functor begins.

L-knowledge-butler.statement: The ideal is to use Luthier alongside the AI as a kind of butler of knowledge.

L-knuth-expressive-languages.statement: Luthier draws the most expressive and natural from lambda calculus, Lisp, C++ and Python, aiming at a language Knuth would like, with code as a first-class citizen.

L-language-for-the-ai.statement: Luthier should be a language used by the AI itself, with the risk that it self-hacks.

L-language-indicates-knowledge.statement: Luthier is thought of as a language that indicates knowledge, in Martin-Löf's reading where a judgment is an act of knowledge and the bodyless hole is an epistemic assumption.

L-language-is-universe.statement: Inventing a programming language is like inventing a universe with its own laws.

L-language-of-ideas.statement: Luthier is a language for defining ideas, where ideas are first-class citizens, like natural languages define things.

L-language-parts-compiler.statement: The language has parts: a grammar with semantic rules and a front compiler to C++.

L-language-self-writing.statement: Defining new types and functions should itself be programmable, the language writing itself, which requires a simple robust language with no syntactic sugar.

L-law-is-type-plus-predicate.statement: A law is a type of arguments together with a predicate over them, so the generator knows what to sample and different laws can quantify over different variables.

L-law-takes-function-as-argument.statement: A law takes the function under test as its first argument and the quantified variables after, so the type it belongs to has any implementation as a term.

L-laws-are-declarations.statement: Laws are ordinary declarations, holes until proven, and falsifiable by an instance that does not type.

L-laws-are-the-normal-form.statement: The novelty is that a group of functions with its laws, as a type whose laws are run by default, is the normal way to define anything, not a separate verification tool.

L-laws-force-decisions.statement: Writing a group's laws forces design decisions, such as what a read of an absent key returns.

L-laws-like-cpp-requires.statement: Laws are written in few lines like a C++ requires block: quantified variables in a header and one Bool expression per line, each a type requirement checked without running or a value requirement run by the test.

L-learn-from-each-run.statement: From each run of the code something is learned, whether an implementation is correct or how fast it is.

L-levels-of-equivalence.statement: A fundamental idea of Luthier is to express different levels of equivalence (same information, isomorphic, exactly equal, same memory location), each a different equivalence functor.

L-levels-of-verification.statement: A value can be untested or tested, with different levels of verification.

L-levels-of-view.statement: From a series of operations one can take different views or levels: the magma, the result, the execution, the code.

L-library-adapter.statement: A library is used by requiring it follow patterns and satisfy propositions defined from Luthier, with an adapter fitting it to each use, so Luthier acts as a universal adapter between libraries.

L-likelihood-type-propagation.statement: Likelihood recursion is encoded via type-theoretic propagation, with noise structures and model boundaries as dependent types.

L-lisp-quote-code-as-data.statement: Writing f a as data within a program uses the Lisp quote '(f a) as sugar, with the parser producing the Term constructors.

L-lisp-single-primitive.statement: Lisp reduces everything to one primitive, lists, as inspiration for reducing Luthier.

L-living-vs-dead-language.statement: Luthier can be a living language that acts or a dead language that only describes; the descriptive role is where it starts.

L-luthier-is-assignments.statement: Luthier is a chain of assignments, each an identifier, an equals sign and an operation that creates the object.

L-luthier-is-extended-concepts.statement: Luthier is C++ concepts extended to the whole language: predicates with semantic requirements that are run and whose results are stored, keeping subsumption and composition.

L-luthier-is-verified-library.statement: Luthier itself is a series of verified types and functions with their theorems and tests, almost an instance of the pattern.

L-luthierize-foreign-code.statement: Luthier annotates and 'luthierizes' foreign code, verifying it against the definition of what it should do within some error.

L-machine-verifiable-theories.statement: HoTTification offers a path toward machine-verifiable biological theories.

L-macroir-consumes-models.statement: MacroIR consumes structurally defined Markov models and computes interval-averaged likelihoods for macroscopic current data.

L-map-to-other-languages.statement: Describe functions and equivalences and map them to other languages (C, C++, Java), not directly but by giving the tools for others to extend the translation.

L-markov-generated.statement: Markov models become generated objects rather than arbitrary inputs.

L-match-is-recursor-sugar.statement: match is not primitive but sugar for the recursor a data declaration gives, the only way to open a data value, and over Bool it is if.

L-mentor-friction.statement: The mentor step produces friction on the design process without designing itself.

L-meta-layer.statement: The language sits as a meta-layer above the ConformationalModel DSL, MacroIR and Bayesian pipelines.

L-meta-recursive.statement: The object of Luthier is to work on Luthier; being meta-recursive, operating on itself from the start, is fundamental.

L-meta-theory-discovery.statement: The final product is a meta-theory of scientific discovery architecture, a unifiable theory-building system, not just new models.

L-minimal-core-primitives.statement: There should be a clear core where all Luthier operations execute, with only a few primitives implemented in C or similar so it runs.

L-minimal-primitives.statement: Open question whether Luthier needs primitive functions or only coordinates external ones, keeping native components minimal, perhaps only identity and equality.

L-minimalism-maximalism.statement: There is no contradiction between minimalism and maximalism: the minimalism is in the few founding components, from which a huge edifice of complex concepts is built.

L-model-of-computation.statement: Luthier contains a model of computation that you keep testing and simplifying and must keep active, through selective forgetting or aggregation, justified by its use on a particular case.

L-modelgraph-parammanager.statement: Clean separation of the ModelGraph and ParameterManager structures.

L-models-as-well-typed-objects.statement: Biological models are well-typed objects where types are molecular states, identity paths are symmetries, and composition emerges from dependent type operations.

L-must-be-useful.statement: Luthier must be useful and take root in something real, not stay purely theoretical, so it hits reality and reveals its limits.

L-name-the-pattern-library.statement: The verification structure the pattern builds is named Library, not Luthier the language; an instance is a program that passed its tests and can show it, so the adjective tested is superfluous.

L-next-recursor-syntax.statement: What to attack next, in order: choose the recursor (without the dependent one there are no general paths proven by induction), then the concrete syntax.

L-no-inheritance-polymorphism.statement: Luthier would not incorporate C++-style derived classes or polymorphism.

L-no-parameterless-lambda.statement: A parameterless lambda should not exist: without time or effects \ () { a + a } and a + a are the same value, a consequence of the commutativity of statements.

L-no-principle-without-example.statement: No principle enters the specification without an example worked by hand in the candidate notation.

L-no-value-without-passing-check.statement: There is no way to hold a value of a subtype without its predicate having been evaluated or proved; the check runs when the value is built.

L-nonunivocal-functions.statement: The language must natively model non-univocal functions, functions with error, samples.

L-numeric-tests-not-logic.statement: The aim of the first version is to generate numeric tests, not to do propositional logic.

L-one-binding-form.statement: One binding form name : Type appears identically in declaration, parameter, dependent type and pair, with A -> B sugar for (_ : A) -> B and the dot disappearing.

L-only-types-and-functions.statement: Luthier collapses the many constructs into a single kind: only types and functions exist, and functions are themselves a type.

L-optimize-own-rules.statement: Since he invents the language it follows his rules, so he can optimize the rules to make manipulating programs easy.

L-original-vs-derivative-types.statement: Some types are original (made from audios and questionnaires) and all the rest are derivative, results of functions, so they necessarily have structure.

L-particle-filtering-paths.statement: The exponential explosion of the path space is handled by particle filtering: running several stochastic programs in parallel exploring different paths.

L-path-cost-estimate.statement: Each execution path carries an estimate of its characteristics: compute time above all, also error, memory, and where it runs.

L-path-equivalence-core.statement: Path equivalence, proving that different implementations are equivalent, is Luthier's fundamental and hardest concept.

L-paths-implementations.statement: One function can be implemented in many ways (paths), each with its own precision and speed, and the equivalence between implementations is seen through the paths.

L-patterns-in-composition.statement: When functions are associative you can find patterns in the composition, such as a loop as a series of functions raised to a power.

L-performance-database.statement: Luthier keeps a database recording, for each function, initial data, scale and algorithm, the measured time, precision and run characterization.

L-pipeline-forgetting.statement: The consolidation cost growing with the corpus is the forget-functor problem applied to the pipeline, to be handled by consolidating in batches or from a previous consolidate.

L-pipeline-method.statement: The working method is the pipeline audios to ideas to consolidation to mentor, and only after that cycle comes writing the specification.

L-pre-formal-safety.statement: Semantic contracts and diagnostics form a pre-formal, soft homotopy layer that structures and defends correctness before hard type checking exists.

L-pre-postconditions.statement: Functions and types are defined by preconditions and postconditions, the postconditions defining the subtype.

L-precondition-is-type.statement: A precondition is guaranteed by the argument's type, checked when the reference is formed; preconditions that are predicates over values require refined types.

L-predicate-concatenation.statement: Predicates concatenate two ways: conjunction where both pass, and refinement where the second is defined over the subtype the first carves and the order is forced.

L-predicate-delimiter-syntax.statement: How to mark where a subtype's predicate begins: the bar is overloaded, so use a dedicated form rather than overload it further.

L-primitives.statement: A proposed set of primitive value types and primitive functions.

L-probabilistic-hott.statement: Proving path equivalence needs a probabilistic extension of HoTT, a marriage of HoTT and Bayes, with an internal prover plus empirical statistical demonstration.

L-probabilities-and-types-together.statement: Probabilities and types should go almost together, the equivalences being probabilistic, with HoTT giving the universe over which the probabilities apply.

L-program-as-function.statement: A Luthier program is modeled first as a pure function (input to output), extendable later to an interactive model, and can take another Luthier program as input.

L-program-inductive-eval.statement: Code and data in the Lisp form: Program is an inductive type and eval a partial function Program → Name → Maybe Term, with no eval injecting arbitrary terms into the type system, which prevents self-hacking.

L-program-not-a-type-in-hott.statement: HoTT models functions and types but not a complete program (a set/series of expressions), a theoretical gap between the part and the whole.

L-projections-reconstruct.statement: Joining all the projections of an object recovers the original object.

L-proof-assistants-verify.statement: Proof assistants (Coq, Lean, Agda) can verify the semantic correctness of biological models via type-checking.

L-proof-capsules.statement: Local safety containers (ScientificSafe<T>, Maybe_error<T>) are validity capsules wrapping high-risk regions.

L-properties-within-error.statement: The properties a function must satisfy (like an inverse recovering the value) hold only within a certain error.

L-proposition-is-type-truth.statement: True/false is not Bool: a proposition is a type, true if it has a term; ⊤ and ⊥ are the extremes and Bool is a datum with two constructors.

L-pyluthier-implementation.statement: A Python implementation carries the type as a floating class attribute, the easiest start, though Python is not a real type tool and the type ends up as fields and decorations.

L-python-spirit.statement: Luthier imitates Python's spirit of expressing human ideas easily (with the Monty Python / Luthier wordplay).

L-quantifiers-first-class.statement: The logical quantifiers for-all and exists should be first-class citizens of Luthier.

L-reasonable-then-wild.statement: His method of thinking is to work out the reasonable version first, then look for the wild move.

L-reasoning-to-code-isomorphism.statement: There should be a one-to-one relation between reasoning and the flow of the code, so running the code verifies the reasoning.

L-records-as-relational-db.statement: What a record is can be stored as a relational database: fields, relations, a record being a subset of the cartesian product with duplicates removed.

L-recover-meaning-as-ai-codes.statement: Since the AI now writes all the code, Luthier is the way to recover contact with meaning and have things guaranteed without looking at the code.

L-recursive-like-lisp.statement: Luthier is imagined as a recursive language like LISP but nicer, with a clear mathematical equivalence for its code.

L-reduction-three-rules.statement: A reduction step has three rules, beta (substitute a lambda), delta (unfold a definition) and iota (run the recursor); the order of the clauses is the evaluation strategy, and another choice gives another trace for the same result.

L-redundancy-crosses-coloneq.statement: The redundancy worth keeping is the one that crosses the := , where type and body say different things the verifier checks; redundancy repeated on one side is removable with sugar.

L-refl-checks-definitional.statement: To assert a definitional equality as a check in a program, write _ : a = b := refl, which types only if a ≡ b, so no extra symbol is needed, and this is what makes the test be the code itself.

L-reject-address-data.statement: Address/data is rejected as a fundamental element: the name is the reference and the memory address is a decoration of the lowest equivalence level, with nothing to distinguish without mutation and time.

L-remaking-foundations.statement: He has re-made the language many times, each time rethinking the foundations of programming more deeply.

L-replace-adhoc-model-spaces.statement: Replace ad hoc model design with compositional, type-safe, generative model spaces.

L-reproducibility-formal.statement: The reproducibility crisis is a lack of structural verification, and reproducibility is a formal property.

L-result-type-closed.statement: Each function declares a result type with fixed fields; the set of result types is open but every individual type is closed, a sum of types, not a JSON blob.

L-run-external-programs.statement: Luthier needs a built-in facility to run external programs and compilers easily.

L-runtime-vs-semantic-safety.statement: Runtime safety prevents crashes while semantic safety, a layer above runtime, prevents invalid models from existing at all.

L-sample-probability-duality.statement: Sample and probability form a duality, with tests demonstrating it holds.

L-sampler-type-indexed.statement: Sampler state spaces and parameter manifolds are treated as type-indexed temperature-ladder manifolds.

L-sav-bridge-to-proof.statement: SAV bridges empirical outputs and tests toward future type-theoretic proofs, a proof proxy whose tests become type-inhabiting witnesses once types are ready.

L-sav-framework.statement: Semantic Adjoint Verification is a lightweight diagnostic framework whose tests are derived from adjoint functor pairs rather than arbitrary unit tests.

L-sav-triangle-identity.statement: An SAV test asserts that composing the diagnostic after the forward map recovers identity up to statistical or structural tolerance.

L-schema-from-type.statement: The storage schema is generated from the function's declared type rather than written by hand, and migration is derived.

L-self-estimation-functions.statement: The time- and precision-modelling functions are themselves written in Luthier and used by Luthier itself.

L-self-extensible.statement: Luthier must be completely self-extensible: you write all of Luthier in Luthier, so only a few primitives are actually implemented.

L-semantic-then-efficient.statement: Once semantic validity and equivalence are established, a clear slow algorithm can be replaced by an efficient equivalent one, enabling optimization.

L-semantic-zones-kernel.statement: A type-theoretic HoTT kernel provides a formal model/inference algebra plus constructible semantic zones for safety.

L-semantics-own-universe.statement: The semantics lives in its own universe, not that of C++, even while using C++ structures to express it.

L-separate-structure-inference.statement: Deterministic structural validity (via HoTT) is kept separate from probabilistic inference (via Bayesian layers), probability handled downstream.

L-separate-type-from-term.statement: The notation f : A -> A := \ (x) { x + x } separating type from term is preferred: instantiation is declaration plus := term, with one way to build functions (the lambda) and one to write their type (the arrow).

L-set-builder-notation.statement: The single subtype form is set-builder notation { pattern : material | predicate }, which denotes a Sigma; mainstream languages omit it because deciding the predicate needs a solver, a proof or a runtime check, and Luthier's fourth way tests it with n cases recorded in the certificate.

L-sharing-platform.statement: Luthier is a platform where sharing your information makes you win, because you learn where you stand relative to the rest.

L-simplify-type-composition.statement: Simplifying the composition of dependent types needs a simplifying typing algebra, not a free monoid, that keeps the resulting type's complexity bounded; a key engineering problem.

L-simultaneous-definition.statement: When postconditions are interdependent, objects are defined together, in tuples with crossconditions, the one form of definition.

L-spec-makes-decisions.statement: The specification is the first document that makes decisions; a decision is recognized because it excludes something that still coexists in the audios.

L-spec-without-implementation.statement: Inspired by Modelica, Luthier separates the specification of a program from its implementation.

L-start-easy-own-language.statement: One can implement Luthier inside a host language starting with the easiest 'kind of Luthier', or make it directly its own language.

L-start-from-reals.statement: Start from the ABC: numbers, the reals, their operations, and a concept of error of the reals.

L-statements-commute.statement: Make statements commutative so their order doesn't change the result, with temporality reconstructed from causal type dependence, trading some expressivity.

L-states-as-type-algebra.statement: States and channels and their multiplicities are represented with type algebra (sum for states, product for channels), with a constructor from a number to a set.

L-substitution-capture.statement: Substitution has a variable-capture problem; the cheap by-hand fix is requiring all bound names distinct and the serious fix is de Bruijn indices (var : N -> Term for bound variables).

L-subtype-by-predicate.statement: A subtype (subObject) is the subset of a type whose values satisfy a predicate, a test.

L-sugar-adds-no-term-constructor.statement: Sugar may add nothing to Term: a construct that forces a new Term constructor is a primitive to discuss, not sugar.

L-sum-types-with-bar.statement: Types are expressed as alternatives with a bar, as in maybe, either and sum.

L-summary-bigger-than-data.statement: A model or summary can end up bigger than the data it summarizes.

L-symbol-economy.statement: A symbol is used only for what appears often with a fixed universal meaning and already exists outside with it; anything rare, content-bearing or without a natural reading is a word, since the language is read aloud and written by hand.

L-symmetry-as-identity-paths.statement: Symmetry reductions are path-based identities that collapse state redundancies into reduced Markov spaces.

L-syntax-declarations-instantiations.statement: Luthier's syntax is reduced to only declarations and instantiations.

L-syntax-semantics-before-implementation.statement: Fix Luthier's syntax and semantics on paper first, and only then implement it.

L-synthesis-is-key.statement: Synthesizing information well is the key to the whole design.

L-synthesize-runs.statement: The accumulated run information must be synthesized over time so it doesn't grow monstrous and paralyzing.

L-term-is-data-syntax.statement: Term is the type of Luthier's syntax defined in Luthier itself with data, one constructor per form of term (including one for data { ... }); code is a first element because syntax is a data like N, making the core self-verifying and metacircular.

L-term-untyped-check.statement: Term is untyped syntax (senseless terms are constructible) and whether a term has sense is decided by check; a Term admitting only well-typed terms exists but is much harder, so raw syntax plus check suffices to start.

L-test-result-one-or-explanation.statement: A check returns success (one) if met or an explanation of why it failed, not just a boolean.

L-tests-as-morphisms.statement: Each CLI operation is a typed morphism and each test a witness path or triangle identity, not a patch.

L-things-guaranteed.statement: Luthier's purpose is better error management and things guaranteed, because having a type means satisfying certain propositions.

L-time-as-dependency.statement: Time, the order of things, is modeled as dependency between definitions, the mathematical way: if one thing depends on another there is a time.

L-time-from-input-features.statement: Compute time is predicted from a simplification of the inputs (the most predictive features, e.g. a matrix's rows and columns); some functions are independent of their inputs.

L-total-vs-partial-guarantee.statement: A law can hold either by conditioning it in the type (total function, partial guarantee) or by restricting the function (partial function, total guarantee), the choice depending on who uses it.

L-truncation-operators.statement: The programmer could use homotopy truncation operators to clean a complex type.

L-two-kinds-of-definition.statement: There are two ways to define types, the constructive and the declarative.

L-two-layers.statement: Luthier has two layers: a first of equivalences and verifiability, and a second that measures time, complexity, resources and success/failure and picks the faster of two equivalent paths.

L-type-autodetection.statement: Types can be handled by autodetection.

L-type-carries-its-laws.statement: A type (or function) carries, as a proposition, the law its values must satisfy.

L-type-definition-recursive.statement: A type's definition is necessarily recursive, since the type must be universally accessible like identifiers.

L-type-inference.statement: The type is deduced by type calculation, and a derived type larger than the parameter's type is flagged.

L-type-is-history.statement: What a type holds is the history of how you arrived at it (e.g. a loop as a combination of types with an exponent).

L-type-safe-priors.statement: Type-safe prior spaces bridge the MacroIR likelihood engine with structural model spaces.

L-types-are-concepts.statement: Types are concepts, types as propositions, and types include functions and higher-order functions.

L-types-make-code-safe.statement: Declaring a function declares the tests it must pass, so types encode preconditions and gate membership on testing, yielding self-verified programs.

L-types-spaces-identities-paths.statement: HoTT gives types as spaces and identities as paths, its internal equality replacing ad hoc isomorphisms.

L-typing-accumulates.statement: Composing dependent functions accumulates a growing typing load, so the decoration can end up far bigger than the value.

L-unevaluated-is-syntactic.statement: "Unevaluated" is not a runtime state like a thunk because there is no time; it is a syntactic datum, which removes any lazy-evaluation semantics.

L-unit-is-group-of-functions.statement: The unit of definition is not a function with a postcondition but a group of functions with the laws relating them; a single function is the group of size one.

L-units-with-parametrizable-requirements.statement: No language ships units that carry a set of requirements they must satisfy; in Luthier the predicate is a function with parameters (max error, scalability), so the certificate states which parameters are met and a dependent library inherits them.

L-universal-type.statement: A universal type comprising the types of all dimensions, like an abstract class, taken as a feasible coding challenge.

L-value-carries-annotations.statement: A value carries an annotation of everything already known about its class.

L-value-knows-operation.statement: A value knows the concrete operation that produced it: the sum is the sum, not the generic magma operation.

L-variable-is-fields.statement: A variable is a name, a memory address, a size and a type; the type contains the size and the name can be the address.

L-variable-not-know-environment.statement: A variable knows its name but should not know its environment, so its resource acquisition stays predictable.

L-verifiability.statement: Luthier must verify that a function is correct; verifiability, with equivalence, is a minimal element of the language.

L-verify-by-sampling.statement: Luthier verifies postconditions by sampling possible inputs, and postcondition verification and coverage calibration are the same computation.

L-von-neumann-epigraph.statement: Luthier's founding epigraph is Von Neumann's: state exactly what a machine supposedly cannot do and he will build a machine that does it.

L-well-defined-dsl.statement: The DSL and the way code is written must be very well defined.

L-what-is-a-program.statement: The basic question of Luthier: what is a Luthier program, a map or a graph?

L-what-is-it-for.statement: Open question of what Luthier is actually for; so far it is an intellectual adventure.
